<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Ceridian Corporation (&#147;Ceridian&#148; or the
&#147;Company&#148;) was formed as a result of the spin-off of
the human resource services division and human resource services
and Comdata subsidiaries of a predecessor entity. On
March&nbsp;30, 2001, Ceridian became an independent public
company when its predecessor distributed all of Ceridian&#146;s
outstanding common stock to the predecessor&#146;s stockholders
in a tax free spin-off transaction (the &#147;spin-off&#148;).
Despite the legal form of the spin-off, because of the
significance of the human resource services and Comdata business
to its predecessor, Ceridian is considered the divesting entity
in the spin-off and is treated as the &#147;accounting
successor&#148; to the predecessor entity (now called
Arbitron&nbsp;Inc.) and will report financial information about
its continuing operations as well as the financial history of
the Arbitron media information business prior to the reverse
spin-off as &#147;discontinued operations.&#148; For further
information, see the note to the consolidated financial
statements entitled &#147;Reverse Spin-Off Transaction.&#148;

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In the opinion of the Company, the unaudited consolidated
financial statements reflect all adjustments (consisting only of
normal recurring accruals, except as set forth in the notes to
consolidated financial statements) necessary to present fairly
the Company&#146;s financial position as of March&nbsp;31, 2001,
and results of operations and cash flows for the three month
periods ended March&nbsp;31, 2001 and 2000.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The results of operations for the three month period ended
March&nbsp;31, 2001 are not necessarily indicative of the
results to be expected for the full year.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The consolidated financial statements should be read in
conjunction with the notes to consolidated financial statements.

<P align="left"><B>Reverse Spin-Off Transaction</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On March&nbsp;30, 2001, all of the outstanding shares of common
stock of New&nbsp;Ceridian Corporation were distributed to the
stockholders of the entity formerly called Ceridian Corporation
(&#147;Old&nbsp;Ceridian&#148;) in a tax-free reverse spin-off
transaction (the &#147;spin-off&#148;). New&nbsp;Ceridian
Corporation comprises the human resource services division and
subsidiaries (&#147;HRS&#148;) and Comdata subsidiaries of
Old&nbsp;Ceridian. As part of the spin-off, Old&nbsp;Ceridian
was renamed Arbitron&nbsp;Inc., and New&nbsp;Ceridian
Corporation was renamed Ceridian Corporation. Despite the legal
form of the spin-off, because of the relative significance of
HRS and Comdata to Old&nbsp;Ceridian prior to the spin-off,
Ceridian is treated as the accounting successor and Arbitron
media information business is treated as the spun-off
discontinued operation in the financial statements of Ceridian.
As used in this report, references to &#147;Ceridian&#148; or
the &#147;Company&#148; mean Ceridian Corporation, formerly
known as New&nbsp;Ceridian Corporation, together with its
consolidated subsidiaries, and include its post-spin financial
results as well as the historical financial results of the
businesses that constituted Old&nbsp;Ceridian prior to the
spin-off.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The spin-off required new financing arrangements for the
Company. Under the terms of agreements related to the spin-off,
Arbitron furnished $225.0 from its own borrowings toward the
retirement of Old&nbsp;Ceridian&#146;s debt outstanding
immediately prior to the spin-off. The $225.0 Arbitron payment,
borrowings of $235.0 under the Company&#146;s January 2001
domestic revolving credit facility and existing cash balances
were used to retire the $430.0 of Old&nbsp;Ceridian&#146;s
senior notes and the $50.0&nbsp;balance under
Old&nbsp;Ceridian&#146;s U.S.&nbsp;revolving credit facility and
pay $26.5 under a &#147;make-whole&#148; provision of the senior
notes agreement that relates to early retirement of the notes
and $1.0 in deferred origination fees in connection with the
January 2001 revolving credit facility. The $225.0 payment
liability, combined with other assets and liabilities of
Arbitron, resulted in net liabilities of discontinued operations
of $182.9 at the time of the spin-off, which increased the
Company&#146;s retained earnings in that amount when the
spin-off took place. Additionally, the par value of the
Company&#146;s common stock was established as $.01&nbsp;per
share, compared to a par value of $.50&nbsp;per share for
Old&nbsp;Ceridian common stock, and no treasury common stock was
distributed to the Company, resulting in a reduction of
additional paid-in capital of $262.2. Further details on
financing and equity transactions are presented in the note to
the consolidated financial statements entitled
&#147;Financing.&#148;

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Earnings from discontinued operations of Arbitron after
July&nbsp;18, 2000 and until the date of the spin-off are first
applied to the reduction of the spin-off charges of $39.4, net
of income taxes. At December&nbsp;31, 2000, the net amount of
spin-off charges was reduced to a loss of $6.9 by applying an
estimated $32.5 expected to be earned by the discontinued
operations prior to the spin-off. The actual earnings of
discontinued operations after July&nbsp;18, 2000 exceeded the
December&nbsp;31, 2000 estimate by $5.2, which reduced the loss
from disposition from $6.9 to $1.7.

<P align="left"><B>Payroll and Tax Filing Client Funds</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In connection with its HRS payroll and tax filing services in
the U.S. and Canada, Ceridian collects funds from clients for
payment of employee compensation and taxes due, holds such funds
in trust until payment is due, and remits the funds to the
appropriate party. For such services, Ceridian derives revenue
from fees charged and from income it receives from the
investment of client funds pending their remittance to settle
client obligations.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
It is the Company&#146;s policy to hold U.S. and Canadian client
fund investments separately in short-term portfolios to provide
liquidity to meet client fund obligations and long-term
portfolios to produce increased investment income through higher
yields to maturity. The short-term portfolios contain money
market securities and other cash equivalents that mature within
90&nbsp;days after purchase and whose acquisition cost

<P align="left">
does not differ materially from fair value. The long-term
portfolios contain U.S.&nbsp;or Canadian government securities,
mortgage- and asset-backed securities rated AAA, and corporate
debt securities rated A3/A- or better. Due to the positive
intent and ability of the Company to hold these securities until
maturity and supporting historical experience, the long-term
portfolios are classified as held-to-maturity and are measured
by amortized cost. Disposition of these securities before
maturity is expected to be limited to unusual circumstances such
as significant deterioration of the issuer&#146;s
creditworthiness or a major business combination or disposition.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
As identified on the consolidated balance sheet, payroll and tax
filing client funds and the offsetting obligations amounted to
$3,513.5 at March&nbsp;31, 2001 and $2,945.0 at
December&nbsp;31, 2000. This amount varies significantly during
the year and averaged $2,227.4 and $2,170.3, respectively, for
the three-month periods ended March&nbsp;31, 2001 and 2000. The
following table provides cost and market price information for
various classifications of client fund investments.

<P align="left"><B>Financing</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Under an agreement with a syndicate of commercial banks dated
January&nbsp;31, 2001, Ceridian entered into a $350.0 domestic
revolving credit facility, of which $50.0 may be used for
letters of credit, that expires in March 2006. The credit
facility is unsecured and its pricing for both loans and letters
of credit is based on Ceridian&#146;s senior unsecured debt
ratings and LIBOR. The interest rate on borrowings under this
facility was 5.5% as of April&nbsp;30, 2001. Under the terms of
the credit facility, Ceridian&#146;s consolidated debt must not
exceed its stockholders&#146; equity as of the end of any fiscal
quarter, and the ratio of Ceridian&#146;s earnings before
interest and taxes to interest expense on a rolling four quarter
basis must be at least 2.75 to 1. The credit facility also
limits liens, subsidiary debt, contingent obligations, operating
leases, minority equity investments and

$235.0 and letters of credit totaling $2.0 remained outstanding,
and the Company was in compliance with all covenants contained
in the credit facility.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
At the time of the spin-off, advances of $235.0 from the January
2001 credit facility, the $225.0 Arbitron payment and existing
cash balances funded the required early retirement of the $430.0
of senior notes outstanding and payment of the $50.0 balance
outstanding under the $250.0 domestic revolving credit facility
dated July&nbsp;1997 at the time of the spin-off. The redemption
of senior notes required a payment of $456.5, which included
$26.5 under a &#147;make-whole&#148; provision of the senior
notes agreement, based on the relationship of the nominal
interest rate of the senior notes to a certain market rate. The
establishment of the 2001 revolving credit facility resulted in
the payment of $1.0 for origination costs that will be amortized
over the term of the facility. In addition, the balance
outstanding on the Canadian revolving credit agreements was
reduced from $19.1 to $15.1 by payments of $4.0 during first
quarter 2001.

<P align="left"><B>Derivative Securities</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Ceridian&#146;s risk management policy is to hedge a substantial
portion of its interest rate exposure from its investment of
client funds, as further described in the note to the
consolidated financial statements entitled &#147;Payroll and Tax
Filing Client Funds,&#148; viewed within the context of
management&#146;s expectation of the future economic
environment. Due to liquidity requirements for client fund
obligations, a large percentage of client funds are held in
overnight-maturing investments that are subject to interest rate
variability. This variability can be offset by purchases of
longer-term instruments and by offsetting the variable rate
income with floating rates on the Company&#146;s debt
obligations. The remaining interest rate risk may be managed
with derivative securities.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
It is the policy of the Company to hold derivative securities
only for the purpose of hedging interest rate risk and not for
speculative activity. Ceridian&#146;s hedging activities may
include the use of interest rate swaps, collars, caps and
floors, primarily with respect to investment of client funds or
its debt obligations. These derivative securities typically
function as cash flow hedges of the designated item.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
At January&nbsp;1, 2001, Ceridian maintained interest rate
collars for the purpose of hedging interest rate risk on
invested client funds. The counterparties to these arrangements
are commercial banks with debt ratings of A or better. These
arrangements, which do not require collateral, require the banks
to pay Ceridian the amount by which a certain index of
short-term interest rates falls below a specified floor strike
level. Alternatively, when that index exceeds a specified cap
strike level, Ceridian is required to pay out the excess above
the cap strike level. The Company is currently hedging its
interest rate exposure over a period not greater than
38&nbsp;months.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Financial Accounting Standard 133, &#147;Accounting for
Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities,&#148; (as
amended) became effective for Ceridian on January&nbsp;1, 2001.
Therefore, at that date, the Company&#146;s interest rate
collars were recorded on its balance sheet at fair value,
resulting in recognition of a liability of $0.4, a credit to
accumulated other comprehensive income of $0.2, an addition to
deferred tax asset of $0.1 and a pre-tax charge to earnings of
$0.5. As of March&nbsp;31, 2001, the interest rate collars were
revalued resulting in a noncurrent asset of $9.1, a credit in
accumulated other comprehensive income of $4.2 and a deferred
tax liability of $2.3. The impact on pre-tax earnings for first
quarter 2001, including the amount recognized at adoption,
amounted to a credit of $2.6, which is reported in other expense
(income). The credit to accumulated other comprehensive income
represents the effective portion of the collar hedges. This
amount will be reclassified to earnings as cash is received or
paid on collar settlements. During the next 12&nbsp;months, the
Company expects to reclassify $2.5 of this amount to earnings as
settlements occur.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During first quarter 2001, Ceridian sold 1,020,000&nbsp;shares
of HotJobs.com,&nbsp;Ltd. Common stock for aggregate proceeds of
$12.3. As of March&nbsp;31, 2001, Ceridian held a balance of
560,023 registered shares of the common stock of
HotJobs.com,&nbsp;Ltd. (159,459 of which remain in escrow until
May&nbsp;2001) that were received in exchange for preferred
stock received in connection with the sale of Resumix,&nbsp;Inc.
in 1998. The fair value for this investment of $5.06&nbsp;per
share (based on quoted market prices) as of March&nbsp;31, 2001
has been recorded in short-term investments with a corresponding
credit, net of deferred income taxes, to unrealized gain on
marketable securities within accumulated other comprehensive
income in stockholders&#146; equity. Gain or loss on these
securities will be recognized as the securities are sold.

<P align="left"><B>Investing Activity</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During the first three months of 2001, net investing inflows
amounted to $13.3, which consisted of $12.3 from the sale of
1,020,000&nbsp;shares of HotJobs.com,&nbsp;Ltd. stock and $1.0
from the July&nbsp;2000 installment sale of a phone resale
business for which the funds were received in January&nbsp;2001.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In March&nbsp;2001, Ceridian entered into an agreement with
Ultimate Software Group,&nbsp;Inc. in which Ceridian is granted
a non-exclusive license to use Ultimate&#146;s UltiPro software
as part of a Web-enabled integrated ASP offering to middle
market Ceridian customers. Ceridian made an up-front payment to
Ultimate of $10.0, half of which is subject to the successful
transfer of technology to Ceridian. The refundable portion is
reported in other noncurrent assets and the non-refundable
portion is reported in purchased software. Following the
technology transfer, Ceridian will pay a monthly fee based on
the number of employees paid using the Ultimate software.
Ceridian may acquire an equity interest in Ultimate through
purchases in the open market or from third parties, subject to a
contractual limitation of 14.99% of Ultimate&#146;s common stock.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Also during the first three months of 2001, capital expenditures
of $35.6 included $7.4 for transaction processing software and
hardware as a result of a decision by Comdata to bring this
activity in-house and terminate an outsourcing contract.

<P align="left"><B>Comprehensive Income (Loss)</B>

<TR>

</TR>

<TR valign="top">
	<TD></TD>
	<TD>
	<I>Unusual Losses (Gains)</I></TD>
</TR>

</TABLE>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During first quarter 2001, Ceridian recognized a gain of $12.3
from the sale of a significant portion of its holdings of
HotJobs.com,&nbsp;Ltd. common stock, as further described in an
accompanying note entitled &#147;Investing Activity.&#148; Also
during first quarter 2001, the Company recorded accrued exit
costs of $6.7, net of recoveries from first quarter 2000 charges
of $3.2 and impairment losses from asset write-offs of $6.1. The
first quarter 2001 accrued exit costs include a $6.6 charge for
the termination by Comdata of an outsourced transaction
processing contract as well as severance costs of $2.3,
representing 250&nbsp;employees, and excess facility costs of
$1.0, related to a planned small business disposition and the
consolidation of certain HRS operations in Boston, Mass. into
operations in Philadelphia, Penn. First quarter 2001 accrued
exit costs were reduced by the recovery of first quarter 2000
estimated HRS severance costs of $3.2 due primarily to a
reduction in the scale of downsizing of the St.&nbsp;Louis,
Missouri customer service operations. The HRS impairment losses
involve the write-off of surplus furniture and equipment, a
reduction of excess costs on a software development project and
the write-off of goodwill related to a small business that
Ceridian plans to sell. The accompanying table provides details
on the initial charges and their disposition.

such material differences are identified and discussed from time
to time in Ceridian&#146;s filings with the Securities and
Exchange Commission, including those factors discussed in this
quarterly report on Form&nbsp;10-Q and discussed in and
incorporated by reference into Ceridian&#146;s Annual Report on
Form&nbsp;10-K for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000, which
factors are also incorporated herein by reference. Such
important factors include implementation and success of plans to
improve performance of U.S.&nbsp;payroll business, government
regulation changes on timing of remittance and interest rate
changes and investment income from customer deposits, ability to
increase revenue from cross-selling efforts and new products,
ability to improve operating margins in Human Resource Services,
customer retention, effecting system upgrades and conversions,
ability to adapt to changing technology, acquisition risks,
competitive conditions, liability as a portability
administrator, changes in government regulations, Comdata&#146;s
relationships with key vendors and suppliers, risks associated
with the Arbitron reverse spin-off, risks associated with
litigation and similar matters, and other factors such as trade,
monetary and fiscal policies and political and economic
conditions. Ceridian undertakes no obligation to correct or
update any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of
new information, future events or otherwise. You are advised,
however, to consult any future disclosure Ceridian makes on
related subjects in future reports to the&nbsp;SEC.</I>

<P align="left"><B>Results of Operations</B>

<DIV>&nbsp;</DIV>

<TABLE width="100%" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0">

<TR>
	<TD width="1%"></TD>
	<TD width="99%"></TD>
</TR>

<TR valign="top">
	<TD></TD>
	<TD>
	<I>Consolidated Results</I></TD>
</TR>

</TABLE>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
For the first quarter of 2001, Ceridian reported net earnings of
$23.1&nbsp;million, or $.16&nbsp;per diluted share of common
stock and earnings from continuing operations of
$17.9&nbsp;million, or $.12&nbsp;per diluted share of common
stock, on revenue of $309.6&nbsp;million. For the first quarter
of 2000, Ceridian reported net earnings of $20.9&nbsp;million,
or $.14&nbsp;per diluted share of common stock, and earnings
from continuing operations of $6.5&nbsp;million, or
$.04&nbsp;per diluted share of common stock, on revenue of
$309.6&nbsp;million. Net earnings for the first quarter of 2001
included a $5.2&nbsp;million reduction of the previously
reported loss from the spin-off of Arbitron and for the first
quarter of 2000 included $14.4&nbsp;million of earnings from the
discontinued operations of Arbitron. Results for the comparative
quarters were significantly affected by unusual items described
in the section of this discussion entitled &#147;Unusual
Items.&#148;

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In the following tables, the amount of acquisition amortization
for the period is presented separately from other selling,
general and administrative expense (&#147;SG&#38;A&#148;),
&#147;R&#38;D expense&#148; represents research and development
costs, &#147;EBIT&#148; represents earnings before interest and
taxes and percentage relationships that are not meaningful are
represented by &#147;NM.&#148; The references to &#147;HRS&#148;
relate to the human resource services division and subsidiaries
of Ceridian, and references to &#147;Other&#148; relate to the
corporate center operations of Ceridian not allocated to the
business segments.

</CENTER>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Consolidated revenue remained at the same level in the first
quarter of 2001 as in the first quarter of 2000. Revenue in HRS
decreased by $0.7&nbsp;million and increased by the same amount
in Comdata. Total costs and expenses decreased by
$17.7&nbsp;million in the quarterly comparison as HRS costs and
expenses decreased by $17.7&nbsp;million and Comdata&#146;s
costs and expenses increased by $3.2&nbsp;million, while a net
decrease of $3.2&nbsp;million in Other costs and expenses
resulted from a higher unusual gain in the 2001 quarter than the
unusual gain recorded in the first quarter of 2000. Cost of
revenue decreased by $1.2&nbsp;million in HRS and
$1.4&nbsp;million in Comdata while SG&#38;A expense (not
including acquisition amortization) increased by
$14.8&nbsp;million in HRS and $1.2&nbsp;million in Comdata.
Research and development expense was little changed between the
comparative quarters, while the change in other expense
(income), primarily representing the unusual items described in
the following section entitled &#147;Unusual Items,&#148;
increased EBIT by $33.5&nbsp;million. Interest income increased
by $0.8&nbsp;million due to a higher aggregate invested cash and
short-term investment balance related to the spin-off. Interest
expense decreased by $0.9&nbsp;million due primarily to
reductions in the average outstanding U.S. and Canadian
revolving credit balances in the comparative quarters. Income
taxes increased by $8.0&nbsp;million primarily due to the
increase in pre-tax earnings. The effective tax rate for the
first quarter of 2001 was 41.0% compared to 40.6% for the first
quarter of&nbsp;2000.

	<TD width="3%"></TD>

<TR valign="top">
	<TD></TD>
	<TD>
	<I>Human Resource Services</I></TD>
</TR>

</TABLE>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Revenue in HRS decreased by $0.7&nbsp;million as revenue
increases totaling $4.4&nbsp;million in HRS operations in Canada
and the United Kingdom and $1.3&nbsp;million in the work/ life
and benefits services businesses were more than offset by a
decrease of $6.4&nbsp;million in the U.S.&nbsp;payroll and
training businesses. There was little change between the
comparative quarters in interest income from investment of
payroll and tax filing client funds included in HRS revenue as
the yield was 5.92% in both periods and the average balance of
invested funds increased 2.6%. As previously announced, Ceridian
committed to adding approximately 160 sales personnel in 2001
and expending approximately $20&nbsp;million in order to build
and compensate the HRS sales force. As of March&nbsp;31, 2001,
the hiring goal for 2001 had essentially been met and
compensation arrangements restructured in an effort to improve
sales performance. Order levels for the first quarter of 2001
improved by approximately 15% over the first quarter 2000 level
and approximately 20% over the level of the fourth quarter of
2000.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The decrease of $17.7&nbsp;million in costs and expenses from
the first quarter of 2000 to the first quarter of 2001 is
largely due to the $30.5&nbsp;million of unusual charges
included in other expense (income) in the first quarter of 2000.
The increase in SG&#38;A&nbsp;expense (not including acquisition
amortization) of $14.8&nbsp;million was due largely to an
increase of $11.0&nbsp;million in selling expense, reflecting
the significant additions to the sales force in
U.S.&nbsp;operations in late 2000 and early 2001, described
above, costs of reorganizing the sales force and higher
compensation levels. General and administrative expense
increased by $3.8&nbsp;million due to management reorganization
costs and higher compensation levels. An increase between the
comparative quarters of $1.8&nbsp;million in
R&#38;D&nbsp;expense was principally related to
U.S.&nbsp;payroll and tax filing product development efforts.
Unusual items of $3.6&nbsp;million were recorded in other
expense (income) during the first quarter of 2001. These items
included $6.2&nbsp;million of unusual charges, net of
recoveries, and a $2.6&nbsp;million gain related to the interest
rate collars on payroll and tax filing client fund investments.
These and first quarter 2000 unusual charges are further
discussed in the following section entitled &#147;Unusual
Items.&#148;

<DIV>&nbsp;</DIV>

<TABLE width="100%" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0">

<TR>
	<TD width="3%"></TD>
	<TD width="97%"></TD>
</TR>

<TR valign="top">
	<TD></TD>
	<TD>
	<I>Comdata</I></TD>
</TR>

</TABLE>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Comdata revenue increased by $0.7&nbsp;million from
$75.8&nbsp;million for the first quarter of 2000 to
$76.5&nbsp;million for the first quarter of 2001. A revenue
increase of $6.6&nbsp;million in the retail cash card business
of the SVS unit was largely offset by the loss of
$4.7&nbsp;million of revenue recorded in the first quarter of
2000 by the phone resale business sold in July 2000. Lower
revenues for permitting and local fueling also limited revenue
growth in the quarterly comparison, as local fueling operations
develops the systems needed to service recently-signed major
customers. Softening general economic conditions have
significantly affected the freight

<P align="center">16

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left">
market, resulting in reduced trucking activity and increased
failures of small trucking firms. Although Comdata&#146;s
business largely comes from larger, better-financed trucking
firms, it is expected that revenue levels will be adversely
impacted if the economic slowdown continues.
</DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Comdata&#146;s costs and expense increased by $3.2&nbsp;million
from the first quarter of 2000 to the first quarter of 2001.
Cost of revenue decreased by $1.4&nbsp;million due primarily to
the net effect of higher SVS sales and sale of the phone resale
business and an unusually high bad debt expense in the first
quarter of 2000. Even though the bad debt provision of
$3.8&nbsp;million for the first quarter of 2001 is lower than
the first quarter 2000 amount, it represents an increase of
approximately 30% over the average quarterly bad debt provision
in 2000. Selling expense changed little between the comparative
quarters. General and administrative expenses increased
$2.7&nbsp;million due largely to an increase of
$1.3&nbsp;million in goodwill and other intangibles amortization
costs resulting from the acquisition of the remaining interest
in SVS in March 2000 and from higher compensation levels and
increased legal and consulting costs. R&#38;D&nbsp;expense
decreased by $0.9&nbsp;million due largely to the termination of
an outsourced transaction processing development arrangement.
Other expense (income) in the first quarter of 2001 included a
$6.6&nbsp;million contract termination charge and in the first
quarter of 2000 included $2.6&nbsp;million of unusual charges
related primarily to facility closures, as further described in
the following section entitled &#147;Unusual Items.&#148; The
first quarter of 2000 also included a minority interest expense
of $0.7&nbsp;million, while the first quarter of 2001 included a
$0.3&nbsp;million gain related to the July 2000 sale of the
phone resale business.

<DIV>&nbsp;</DIV>

	<I>Other</I></TD>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Other includes the unallocated amounts related to the corporate
center operations of Ceridian. The reported EBIT for the first
quarter of 2001 relates to the $12.3&nbsp;million gain from the
sale of marketable securities described in the notes to the
consolidated financial statements entitled &#147;Short-Term
Investments&#148; and &#147;Investing Activity.&#148; The
reported EBIT for the first quarter of 2000 relates to the
recovery of accruals in the amount of $10.0&nbsp;million from
unusual charges recorded in 1997, reduced by $0.9&nbsp;million
of severance costs included in the first quarter 2000 unusual
charges. Further details on unusual charges and recoveries are
provided in the note to the consolidated financial statements
entitled &#147;Other Expense (Income).&#148;

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The gain on sale of marketable securities of $12.3&nbsp;million
relates to the sale of 1,020,000&nbsp;shares of
HotJobs.com,&nbsp;Ltd. received in 2000 in connection with
Ceridian&#146;s sale of a business in 1998, as further described
in the notes to the consolidated financial statements entitled
&#147;Short-Term Investments&#148; and &#147;Investing
Activity.&#148; The gain from derivative securities relates to
the adoption of Financial Accounting Standard No.&nbsp;133,
&#147;Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging
Activities,&#148; as amended, which is further described in the
note to the consolidated financial statements entitled
&#147;Derivative Securities.&#148;

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The first quarter 2001 accrued exit costs and asset write-downs
resulted from management decisions by Comdata in
February&nbsp;2001 to bring certain transaction processing
operations in-house and by HRS in March 2001 to consolidate
certain work/ life employee assistance operations located in
Boston, Mass. into a similar operation in Philadelphia, Penn.,
prepare a small business for sale, and write off excess costs
related to a software development project. The accrued exit
costs of $6.7&nbsp;million include $6.6&nbsp;million for
termination by

<P align="center">17

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left">
Comdata of an outsourced transaction processing contract (paid
during first quarter 2001), severance costs of $2.3&nbsp;million
(representing 250&nbsp;employees) and excess occupancy costs
(primarily from idled leased space) of $1.0&nbsp;million.
Recoveries of $3.2&nbsp;million relate primarily to a reduction
in the scale of downsizing of the HRS St.&nbsp;Louis, Missouri
customer service operations. The asset write-downs of
$6.1&nbsp;million included $1.1&nbsp;million for surplus
furniture and equipment, $1.9&nbsp;million of goodwill and
$3.1&nbsp;million of software and development cost. The
impairment of goodwill was determined by comparing the
unamortized goodwill that related to the employee training
business to the undiscounted cash flows that was expected to be
received over the amortization period. The impairment of
software and development costs resulted from the decision to
enter into a software licensing agreement with Ultimate Software
Group,&nbsp;Inc. to provide payroll services to middle-market
Ceridian customers rather than to develop such a software
product internally. The amount of the write-down was determined
by comparing the project carrying cost to the recoverable value
of the hardware and developed software used in the project.
Further information on these activities is presented in the note
to the consolidated financial statements entitled &#147;Other
Expense (Income).&#148;
</DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
First quarter 2000 results reflected $44.7&nbsp;million of
unusual charges, reduced by the recovery of $14.2&nbsp;million
of accruals from unusual charges in prior years to a net charge
of $30.5&nbsp;million. Of the $44.7&nbsp;million of unusual
pre-tax charges, $41.2&nbsp;million related to HRS and primarily
to initiatives to improve customer service and the quality of
operations in the U.S.&nbsp;payroll business during 2000. The
remaining $3.5&nbsp;million related to similar activities in
Comdata and corporate center operations. The unusual charges are
comprised of $26.4&nbsp;million of accrued exit costs and
$18.3&nbsp;million of asset write-downs. The accrued exit costs
initially included $16.4&nbsp;million of severance costs and
$10.0&nbsp;million of other exit costs (primarily from idled
leased space). As of March&nbsp;31, 2001, payments of
$10.6&nbsp;million and recoveries of $3.2&nbsp;million had
reduced the accrued severance costs to a balance of
$2.6&nbsp;million. At the same date, payments of
$7.3&nbsp;million had reduced the accrued other exit costs to a
balance of $2.7&nbsp;million.

<P align="center">18
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Cash and equivalents decreased by $45.3&nbsp;million to
$73.2&nbsp;million during the first quarter of 2001 due to the
use of operating cash flows and cash balances to fund investing
and financing activities. While earnings from continuing
operations in the current quarter were $11.4&nbsp;million above
first quarter 2000 earnings, reduction in impairment losses plus
the gains on marketable and derivative securities do not affect
operating cash flows. Therefore, cash flows from continuing
operations earnings declined by $11.0&nbsp;million. Working
capital activities of continuing operations used
$10.4&nbsp;million during the first quarter of 2001, an increase
in cash used of $3.6&nbsp;million in the quarterly comparison.
This change reflects a liquidation of receivables of
$11.4&nbsp;million in the current quarter, compared to build-up
of receivables of $22.5&nbsp;million in the first quarter of
2000. The $33.9&nbsp;million increase in cash provided by
receivables related to Comdata activities and is offset in part
by a decrease of $18.6&nbsp;million in cash provided by Comdata
drafts payable. The relationship of the period-end date and the
timing of weekly draft clearing operations at Comdata
significantly affect the amount of drafts payable and
receivables outstanding. Payments of spin-off costs in the first
quarter of 2001, compared to increases in accruals for first
quarter 2000 unusual charges in the prior year&#146;s quarter,
also reduced cash flows from continuing operations working
capital activities.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Investing cash flows in the first quarter of 2001 included
capital expenditures of $12.0&nbsp;million for property and
equipment and $23.6&nbsp;million for software and development
costs. Of these expenditures, $5.0&nbsp;million for purchased
software and $2.4&nbsp;million for equipment related to
Comdata&#146;s decision to bring its transaction processing
in-house and terminate an existing outsourcing contract. The
increase in software expenditures also reflected milestone
billings received during the first quarter of 2001 for the
ongoing implementation of a purchased accounting system for
HRS&nbsp;operations. First quarter 2001 investing cash flows
also included an advance of $10.0&nbsp;million to Ultimate
Software Group,&nbsp;Inc. to acquire a non-exclusive license to
use their software product to provide middle-market payroll
processing services to Ceridian customers, beginning in early
2002. Half of the payment is refundable, subject to the
successful transfer of technology to Ceridian. The refundable
portion is reported in other noncurrent assets and the
non-refundable portion is reported in purchased software. When
the software is marketed to Ceridian customers, Ceridian will
pay a monthly fee based on the number of employees paid using
the licensed software. The sale of 1,020,000&nbsp;shares of the
common stock of HotJob.com,&nbsp;Ltd. during the first quarter
of 2001 provided proceeds of $12.3&nbsp;million, as further
described in the notes to the consolidated financial statements
entitled &#147;Short-Term Investments&#148; and &#147;Investing
Activity.&#148; Net investing cash outflows in the first quarter
of 2000 of $22.8&nbsp;million related principally to capital
expenditures and included $12.9&nbsp;million of construction in
progress for the new Ceridian headquarters and the renovation of
an office facility used by the benefits services operations of
HRS.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Financing activities in the first quarter of 2001 largely
involved transactions related to the spin-off, further described
in the notes to the consolidated financial statements entitled
&#147;Reverse Spin-Off Transaction&#148; and
&#147;Financing.&#148; At the time of the spin-off, advances of
$235.0&nbsp;million from the January 2001 credit facility, the
$225.0&nbsp;million Arbitron payment and existing cash balances
funded the required early retirement of the $430.0&nbsp;million
of senior notes outstanding and payment of the
$50.0&nbsp;million balance outstanding under the
$250.0&nbsp;million domestic revolving credit facility dated
July 1997 at the time of the spin-off. The redemption of senior
notes required a payment of $456.5&nbsp;million, which included
$26.5&nbsp;million under a &#147;make-whole&#148; provision of
the senior notes agreement, based on the relationship of the
nominal interest rate of the senior notes to a certain market
rate. The establishment of the 2001 revolving credit facility
resulted in the payment of $1.0&nbsp;million for origination
costs that will be amortized over the term of the facility. In
addition, the balance outstanding on the Canadian revolving
credit agreements was reduced from $19.1&nbsp;million to
$15.1&nbsp;million by payments of $4.0&nbsp;million during first
quarter 2001. Financing cash flows in the first quarter of 2000
included the repurchase on the open market of $20.0&nbsp;million
face amount of senior notes and payments under the Canadian
revolving credit facilities.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The $225.0&nbsp;million payment liability, combined with other
assets and liabilities of Arbitron, resulted in net liabilities
of discontinued operations of $182.9&nbsp;million at the time of
the spin-off, which increased the Company&#146;s retained
earnings in that amount when the spin-off took place.
Additionally, the par value of Ceridian&#146;s common stock was
established as $.01&nbsp;per share compared to $.50&nbsp;per
share prior to the spin-off and the Company&#146;s treasury
common stock was eliminated, resulting in a reduction of
additional paid-in

<P align="center">19

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left">
capital of $262.2&nbsp;million. Further details on financing and
equity transactions are presented in the notes to the
consolidated financial statements entitled &#147;Reverse
Spin-Off Transaction&#148; and &#147;Stockholders&#146;
Equity.&#148;
</DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Ceridian has available $113.0&nbsp;million under its domestic
revolving credit agreement that continues until March 2006 that,
along with cash balances and expected positive operating cash
flows, are expected to meet its planned needs for capital
expenditures and acquisitions during 2001.

<P align="left"><B>ITEM&nbsp;3.&nbsp; <I>Quantitative and Qualitative
Disclosures About Market Risk</I></B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
There have been no material changes in the Company&#146;s market
risk during the three-month period ended March&nbsp;31, 2001.
For additional information on market risk, refer to
Part&nbsp;II, Item&nbsp;7A, Quantitative and Qualitative
Disclosure About Market Risk, contained in the Company&#146;s
Annual Report on Form&nbsp;10-K for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Ceridian&#146;s exposure to other forms of market risk,
including foreign exchange risk, is negligible. Foreign
operations consist of payroll and human resource operations in
Canada and the U.K. These foreign operations serve their
respective domestic markets, with all revenues and expenses
denominated in local currency. Other intercompany charges
between U.S. and non-U.S. based operations are not material.
Translation adjustments on investments in foreign operations are
reported in comprehensive income, and are not hedged.
